stem.text: The structure of a mitochondrion is related to its function in respiration.
Figure 9.1 is a diagram of a mitochondrion.

explanation.text: Mitochondria compartmentalise respiratory reactions. The inner membrane holds electron carriers and ATP synthase, while the matrix contains enzymes of the link reaction and Krebs cycle.

reasoningChain: Match labelled structures to their biochemical roles.
Explain membrane surface area and separation of the proton compartments.

stem.text: Table 9.1 shows the mean percentage of cell volume occupied by mitochondria in three different cell types.
Suggest why the three cell types shown in Table 9.1 have different mean percentages of cell volume occupied by mitochondria.

points.text: idea that more active the cell means more mitochondria ;
idea that heart muscle (cell) contraction needs lots of ATP ;
liver cell carries out, glycogenolysis / glycogenesis / gluconeogenesis / deamination / detoxification, so needs ATP ;
idea that red blood cells need room for haemoglobin ;

explanation.text: Mitochondrial volume reflects demand for aerobic ATP, not simply cell size. Continually contracting heart cells have high demand, while mature red blood cells have no mitochondria and rely on glycolysis.

reasoningChain: Compare the work done by each cell type.
Link sustained ATP demand to mitochondrial abundance.

stem.text: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and produces pyruvate which, in aerobic conditions, can enter the mitochondrion.
Outline how a molecule of glucose is converted to molecules of pyruvate during glycolysis.

points.text: glucose phosphorylated by ATP to form fructose (1,6-)bisphosphate ;
fructose (1,6-)bisphosphate splits into two molecules of, triose phosphate / TP ; R hydrolysed

explanation.text: Two ATP are invested in phosphorylation before the six-carbon sugar splits. Oxidation of the resulting triose phosphates reduces NAD and generates ATP as pyruvate is formed.

reasoningChain: Trace phosphorylation and splitting into two three-carbon molecules.
Describe oxidation, reduced NAD formation and ATP production.
